question: Among the second period elements the actual ionization enthalpies are in the order Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne. Be has a higher first ionisation enthalpy (ΔᵢH) than B because
option1: B has a larger atomic radius than Be
option2: Be has a stable, fully-filled 2s² configuration, so more energy is required to remove an electron from it than from the 2p¹ electron of B, which is less penetrating and more shielded from the nucleus
option3: Be has a lower nuclear charge than B
option4: B has a completely filled valence shell
correct_option: Be has a stable, fully-filled 2s² configuration, so more energy is required to remove an electron from it than from the 2p¹ electron of B, which is less penetrating and more shielded from the nucleus

subject: Chemistry
unit: Unit 9 - Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Among the second period elements the actual ionization enthalpies are in the order Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne. O has a lower first ionisation enthalpy (ΔᵢH) than N and F because
option1: oxygen has a larger atomic radius than nitrogen and fluorine
option2: nitrogen has a stable, half-filled 2p³ configuration, so removing an electron from oxygen's paired 2p⁴ configuration is comparatively easier due to inter-electronic repulsion between the paired electrons
option3: oxygen has fewer valence electrons than nitrogen
option4: oxygen has a lower nuclear charge than nitrogen and fluorine
correct_option: nitrogen has a stable, half-filled 2p³ configuration, so removing an electron from oxygen's paired 2p⁴ configuration is comparatively easier due to inter-electronic repulsion between the paired electrons
topic: Ionisation enthalpy deviation (O vs N, F)

subject: Chemistry
unit: Unit 9 - Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: How would you explain the fact that the first ionization enthalpy of sodium is lower than that of magnesium, but its second ionization enthalpy is higher than that of magnesium?
option1: After losing one electron, Na⁺ achieves a stable noble gas (Ne) configuration, so removing a second electron from this stable core requires very high energy; Mg⁺, however, still has one electron left in the 3s orbital, which is comparatively easy to remove
option2: Na has a higher nuclear charge than Mg
option3: Mg has more valence electrons than Na, making removal of its second electron easier
option4: This is an experimental anomaly with no valid explanation
correct_option: After losing one electron, Na⁺ achieves a stable noble gas (Ne) configuration, so removing a second electron from this stable core requires very high energy; Mg⁺, however, still has one electron left in the 3s orbital, which is comparatively easy to remove

subject: Chemistry
unit: Unit 9 - Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: What are the various factors due to which the ionization enthalpy of the main group elements tends to decrease down a group?
option1: Decreasing atomic radius and increasing effective nuclear charge
option2: Increasing atomic size, increased shielding by inner electron shells, and the consequent decrease in effective nuclear charge experienced by the outermost electron
option4: Decreasing number of electrons down the group
correct_option: Increasing atomic size, increased shielding by inner electron shells, and the consequent decrease in effective nuclear charge experienced by the outermost electron
topic: Factors decreasing IE down a group

question: The first ionization enthalpy values (in kJ mol⁻¹) of group 13 elements are: B = 801, Al = 577, Ga = 579, In = 558, Tl = 589. This deviation from the general trend (of decreasing IE down a group) can be explained by
option1: the presence of filled inner d (and f, for Tl) orbitals in Ga, In and Tl, which provide poor shielding of the outer electron from the increased nuclear charge, disrupting the expected smooth decrease
option2: a continuous increase in atomic radius from B to Tl with no real deviation
option3: Ga, In and Tl having completely different valence shell configurations from B and Al
option4: experimental errors in the measured values
correct_option: the presence of filled inner d (and f, for Tl) orbitals in Ga, In and Tl, which provide poor shielding of the outer electron from the increased nuclear charge, disrupting the expected smooth decrease

option2: Negative and more negative than the first

subject: Chemistry
unit: Unit 9 - Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: What is the basic difference between the terms electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity?
option1: Electron gain enthalpy is the energy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron (expressed in kJ mol⁻¹), while electronegativity is a relative measure (with no fixed units) of an atom's tendency to attract the shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond
option2: Electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity are the same property expressed in different units
option3: Electron gain enthalpy applies only to metals while electronegativity applies only to non-metals
option4: Electron gain enthalpy is a property of neutral atoms while electronegativity is a property of ions
correct_option: Electron gain enthalpy is the energy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron (expressed in kJ mol⁻¹), while electronegativity is a relative measure (with no fixed units) of an atom's tendency to attract the shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond

subject: Chemistry
unit: Unit 9 - Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: How would you react to the statement that the electronegativity of N on the Pauling scale is 3.0 in all nitrogen compounds?
option1: The statement is correct, because electronegativity is a fixed atomic property
option2: The statement is incorrect; electronegativity is not an invariant property of an atom — it depends on the hybridisation state of the atom and the nature of the atom(s) it is bonded to, so it can vary from one nitrogen compound to another
option3: The statement is correct only for ionic nitrogen compounds
option4: The statement is incorrect because nitrogen does not have a defined electronegativity value
correct_option: The statement is incorrect; electronegativity is not an invariant property of an atom — it depends on the hybridisation state of the atom and the nature of the atom(s) it is bonded to, so it can vary from one nitrogen compound to another
topic: Electronegativity is not a fixed atomic constant

question: The theory associated with the radius of an atom is that when it (a) gains an electron and (b) loses an electron, respectively, its radius
option1: (a) decreases because electron-electron repulsion decreases ; (b) increases because effective nuclear charge decreases
option2: (a) increases due to increased electron-electron repulsion among a greater number of electrons for the same nuclear charge ; (b) decreases due to increased effective nuclear charge per remaining electron
correct_option: (a) increases due to increased electron-electron repulsion among a greater number of electrons for the same nuclear charge ; (b) decreases due to increased effective nuclear charge per remaining electron
topic: Radius change on gaining/losing an electron

subject: Chemistry
unit: Unit 9 - Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Would you expect the first ionization enthalpies for two isotopes of the same element to be the same or different?
option1: Different, because isotopes have different atomic masses
option2: Same, because isotopes of an element have identical electronic configurations and the same nuclear charge (number of protons), and ionisation enthalpy depends on these factors, not on the number of neutrons
option3: Different, because isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, which affects the nuclear charge
option4: Same, but only if the isotopes have the same mass number
correct_option: Same, because isotopes of an element have identical electronic configurations and the same nuclear charge (number of protons), and ionisation enthalpy depends on these factors, not on the number of neutrons

subject: Chemistry
unit: Unit 9 - Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: What are the major differences between metals and non-metals?
option1: Metals are electropositive (tend to lose electrons, have low ionisation enthalpy, form basic oxides, are good conductors, and are generally malleable/ductile); non-metals are electronegative (tend to gain electrons, have high ionisation enthalpy, form acidic oxides, are poor conductors, and are generally brittle)
option2: Metals tend to gain electrons and form acidic oxides, while non-metals tend to lose electrons and form basic oxides
option3: Metals and non-metals have essentially identical physical and chemical properties
option4: Metals always exist in the gaseous state while non-metals always exist as solids
correct_option: Metals are electropositive (tend to lose electrons, have low ionisation enthalpy, form basic oxides, are good conductors, and are generally malleable/ductile); non-metals are electronegative (tend to gain electrons, have high ionisation enthalpy, form acidic oxides, are poor conductors, and are generally brittle)
